chunks: Inductor saturation. The question: What happens when an inductor saturates?
Saturation is when an inductor's magnetic core is full and cannot hold any more magnetic flux. Up to that point, the core multiplies the inductance.
Past it, the inductance collapses, and the coil behaves like a much smaller inductor. The current then shoots up fast, which can damage other parts in the circuit.
Think of a sponge soaking up water. A dry sponge soaks up a lot, so it does its job well. Once it is completely soaked, more water just runs off.
A core is the sponge, and the magnetic flux is the water. Past the point of fullness, extra current gets almost no help from the core.
The analogy is loose about one thing: some cores fill up gradually, and others hit their limit suddenly.
The steep initial slope is high permeability: lots of flux for little current. Past a few hundred A/m the curve flattens at B sat, and adding more H only adds flux at air's slope.
The inductor's L is proportional to this slope.
Magnetic flux: the amount of magnetic field passing through the coil and core. Core: the magnetic material, such as ferrite, that the wire wraps around.
Saturation current ( I sat ): the current at which the inductance has dropped by a set amount.
Peak current: the highest current the inductor sees, which is what you must compare to I sat .
Slope of current: di over dt equals V over L , so a smaller L means a faster current rise.
Apply 10 volts across a 10 microhenries inductor. The current rises at V over L equals 10 over 0. 00001 equals 1 amps per µs.
Now suppose the core saturates and the inductance falls to 2 microhenries. The same 10 volts now makes the current rise at 5 amps per µs, five times faster.
In a buck converter (a circuit that switches a coil on and off to step a voltage down), the switch would see a sharp current spike. That is the whole idea.
"Saturation is when the core's flux density hits its material limit: the magnetic domains are all aligned, permeability collapses toward that of air, and inductance drops sharply.
Since di over dt equals V over L , the current then ramps much faster and spikes.
That overstresses switches, trips current limits and adds heat, which in ferrite lowers the saturation current further.
So you size an inductor's I sat above the worst-case peak current, DC plus half the ripple, with margin and at temperature."
